characters: Abeiku: an 11-year-old boy in a yellow shirt and brown shorts, with a scuffed notebook.
Naomi: his cousin, 11, in a red dress with two thick braids, who loves facts.
Madam Quansah: the science teacher, in a green dress, carrying a long rope with knots.
The hen: a speckled brown hen with a red comb and a calm stare.
Fossil drawings: a long-necked plant-eating dinosaur skeleton and a chicken skeleton side by side.

narrationPlan.voice: Lively, curious voice with a little humour for the hen
narrationPlan.pace: Energetic and curious, slowing for the big numbers (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Light adventure strings with a comic clucking motif (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Village hens are a familiar sight across Ghana and give learners a close link to dinosaurs.
Dinosaur fossils have been found in other African countries, such as Niger and Egypt; the story does not claim any dinosaur has been found in Ghana.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Confirm with a palaeontologist: the 66 million-year date, the asteroid explanation, the Jobaria age and the “birds are living dinosaurs” statement.
Check whether a more recent Spinosaurus discovery should be mentioned.
Is the claim that Jobaria was found in “the same part of Africa” suitably cautious?

teacherGuide.overview: A story built on a surprising claim. Learners test it by scaling deep time to a rope and then see that birds are living dinosaurs. The rope walk makes huge numbers feel real.
learningGoals: Place events in deep time using a scale.
Explain what happened about 66 million years ago and which dinosaurs survived.
beforeReading: Ask: what is the biggest animal you have ever seen? What do you think lived here long ago?
whileReading: At pages 3 and 4, ask learners to calculate the rope positions before reading.
afterReading: Walk a 150 m scale on the school field with event cards.
Compare a chicken wing or drawing with a theropod diagram.
discussion: Why did the children use a rope?
Why does the hen count as a dinosaur?
reflection: Which fact from the story would you most like to check yourself?

mathsExtension.task: On the rope (1 m = 1 million years), where do humans (300,000 years) fall?
How many years between Jobaria (135 million years ago) and the big extinction (66 million years ago)?
How many times older is the big extinction (66 million years) than our species (300,000 years)?

support: Use a shorter scale, such as 1 cm for every million years on a long paper strip.
stretch: Choose another scale and recalculate the positions. Explain why a good scale makes the numbers easy to compare.

culturalNotes: Village hens are a familiar sight across Ghana and give learners a close link to dinosaurs.
Dinosaur fossils have been found in other African countries, such as Niger and Egypt; the story does not claim any dinosaur has been found in Ghana.
localiseThis: If you cannot lay out 150 m, use a hallway with a scale of 1 cm per million years and mark the main events.
Keep the walk away from roads.

whatWeKnow: Non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago after an asteroid impact.
Birds are descended from theropod dinosaurs and are living dinosaurs.
Jobaria, a plant-eating dinosaur, lived in what is now Niger about 135 million years ago.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Which dinosaurs lived in different parts of Africa, because large areas have been explored very little.
How different groups of dinosaurs lived and moved.

investigation.title: The deep-time rope
materials: A 150 m rope or measuring tape (or a long paper strip)
steps: Decide the scale: 1 m for 1 million years.
Place markers for Homo sapiens (30 cm), the Lake Bosumtwi crater (about 1.07 m), the big extinction (66 m) and Jobaria (135 m).
Walk the rope and talk about what you notice.
investigation.whatToNotice: People appear in the very first step, and dinosaurs are far away in time.
investigation.safetyNote: Do the walk in a safe area away from traffic and in the shade if possible.

factCheck.claim: Jobaria tiguidensis, a plant-eating sauropod, lived in what is now Niger about 135 million years ago; about 50 specimens were found at one site.
factCheck.explanation: From Penn State’s Earth 105 course page on African geology.
factCheck.reference: Penn State EARTH 105, “Africa Geologic History and Paleontology”.

factCheck.claim: The first Spinosaurus fossils were found in Egypt in 1912 and destroyed in a 1944 bombing raid.
factCheck.explanation: From the same course page. Later discoveries may have added new material.
factCheck.reference: Penn State EARTH 105; check recent literature.

factCheck.claim: About 66 million years ago an asteroid impact led to the extinction of all dinosaurs except birds, and birds descended from theropod dinosaurs.
factCheck.explanation: Standard palaeontology, not verified from a named page in this session.
factCheck.reference: Natural History Museum (London) or Smithsonian resources (to verify).

pronunciation.guidance: "HAW-maw" (with open o vowels, as in Homowo).

reviewerNotes: Confirm local Ashanti Twi pronunciation and spelling preference.
